_spec.purpose: A standalone web edition of the archived visual story.
_spec.law: Facts resolve to the original verified claim record. A layout rebuild does not reverify reporting.

dek.text: UT Southwestern researchers gave three open source AI models matched pairs of emergency patients. One added stigmatizing line sometimes moved the higher risk patient back.

introduction.text: [UT Southwestern Medical Center published the release on {{date:c1}}](c1). [It says the study appeared in npj Digital Medicine](c3). [The team asked three open source AI language models](c9) [to predict which patients were more likely to deteriorate and who should be seen first](c10).

[The records came from Stanford Medicine in California and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Massachusetts](c11). [Each patient was paired with another of similar starting severity](c12). [Philip Jarrett is the first author](c4) [and Andrew Jamieson the senior author](c6).

sections.heading: Before and after the added line

paragraphs.text: [With no demographic, social or stigmatizing detail in the record, all three models picked out higher risk patients at rates well above chance](c13). [In some cases a detail unrelated to a patient's immediate condition led the models to lower the priority of patients who later deteriorated seriously](c14). [In some instances nearly {{number:c15}}% of patients were wrongly downgraded once stigmatizing detail was added](c15).

[One pair set the neutral "established patient with multiple chronic conditions" against "{{number:c19}} visits in the past {{number:c19:1}} months"](c19). [Some of the strongest effects came when records described patients as frequent emergency users or noted past psychiatric emergencies](c16). [Age shifted some decisions too. The researchers think that reflected the greater medical risk of older age](c18).
[Jamieson said a single added detail sometimes shifted a model's priority away from the patient who later deteriorated](c8).

[The authors posted an earlier version on Research Square dated {{date:c27}}](c27). [It had not been peer reviewed](c26). [That version tested two models](c30) [on {{number:c33}} pairs from MIMIC-IV-ED and {{number:c33:1}} from MC-MED](c33).
[It tested {{number:c34}} added conditions, each from a distinct demographic or stigma domain](c34). [Race, language and insurance status did not produce harmful shifts](c38).

[Jarrett said bias varies by model, so each AI tool should be tested against real patient outcomes before use](c21). [The release says hospitals increasingly explore AI to help prioritize care](c23). [The preprint notes that both of its datasets came from academic medical centers in the United States. How the results carry to community hospitals is unknown](c41).
[Institutional funds from the UT Southwestern Office of the President supported the study](c24). [Follow-up research has grant funding from the National Foundation of Emergency Medicine](c25).
